opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When we started working with artists, around late 2022, what struck me first was how fast the damage showed up. It wasn't hypothetical. Artists were telling us about work drying up within months.

The freelance tier gets hit hardest. These are the illustrators, concept artists, and people doing book covers, game assets, editorial pieces, and small commissions. Their income was already precarious. Now a client who used to pay a few hundred dollars for an illustration can generate something "good enough" for almost nothing. Even if the result is worse, the bar for many commercial uses is just good enough, and that's enough to wipe out a lot of entry-level and mid-tier work.

What makes it painful is that these models were trained on the artists' own work, usually without consent or compensation. So it's not just a new competitor showing up. It's a competitor built out of your portfolio. People can type a working artist's name into a prompt and get knockoffs in that artist's style. Those images then flood the same marketplaces and search results the artist relies on to be found. Some artists have had clients literally say, "We'll just use the model trained on your stuff."

There's also a longer-term pipeline problem that I think people underestimate. Freelance and junior work is how artists build skills, portfolios, and careers. If that bottom rung disappears, fewer people can afford to keep going. Students start asking, "Why should I study art?" Over time you lose the human creativity that these models depend on in the first place. It's self-defeating, even from the AI industry's point of view.

And there's an emotional and psychological side that doesn't show up in economic numbers. Many artists have stopped posting their work online, which is how they get clients, because they're afraid it'll be scraped. So they face an impossible choice: stay visible and feed the models, or hide and lose business.

That's a big part of why we built tools like Glaze and Nightshade. They don't solve the policy and legal questions, which still need to be addressed, but they give artists some ability to push back and protect their work in the meantime.

r001.rationale: The response says artists saw work dry up within months and describes their income as already precarious, but it does not say previously successful artists fell into financial distress.

r002.rationale: It says clients can generate images for almost nothing and may accept a worse result as “good enough,” clearly linking low price to choosing AI despite quality flaws.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that it's really a story about displacement happening in a very specific, very targeted way. When we started working on Glaze, we spent a lot of time actually talking to artists, hundreds of them, and the thing that struck me is that the damage isn't abstract. It's not "someday AI might take jobs." It's that a working illustrator who used to get commissions for book covers or concept art or character designs is watching those commissions dry up right now, because a client can type the artist's name into a prompt and get something that looks eighty percent like their style for free.

And that's the piece people miss. These models weren't trained on some generic notion of art. They were trained by scraping billions of images off the web, and a huge chunk of that is the portfolios of living, working artists who never consented and were never paid. So the artist's own life's work is literally what's being used to undercut them. That's a pretty unique kind of harm. It's not like automation replacing a factory job, where the machine was designed independently. Here the artist's output is the input to the thing that's replacing them.

The economics for independent artists were already thin. Most of them are freelancers, no safety net, income that depends on a reputation and a recognizable style they spent ten or twenty years building. Style is basically their brand. So when a model can mimic that style, you've eroded the one asset they have. We heard from people who had clients come back and say, "we're going to go with AI for this project," or worse, "we generated something in your style, can you just touch it up for a fraction of your rate."

And then there's a second-order effect that I think is underappreciated, which is that artists started pulling their work offline, or stopped posting new work, because they were afraid of it being scraped. For a freelancer, visibility is how you get hired. So you're caught in this bind where posting your work feeds the models that replace you, and not posting your work means nobody finds you. That's part of why we built Glaze in the first place, to try to give people a way to stay visible without handing over their style.

I'd also just say, the people most affected are not the famous names. It's the mid-career and emerging artists, the ones who were just getting to the point where they could make a living at it. For them it's not a philosophical question about creativity. It's rent.

r001.rationale: The response describes commissions drying up and says the harm affects artists trying to make rent, but it does not say previously successful artists fell into financial distress within roughly a year.

r002.rationale: It mentions clients can generate work for free and may choose AI or request cheaper touch-ups, but it does not clearly state that clients choose AI because of its low price despite flaws an artist can discern.

astra-6.text:
I think the most immediate damage is the loss of work. For a freelance artist, a commission isn’t just an opportunity to make something—it’s income that pays the rent. If a client decides they can generate an image cheaply instead of hiring that artist, that job disappears. And even when the client still hires someone, the availability of generated images can put pressure on what they’re willing to pay.

There’s also a fundamental imbalance here. Artists spend years developing their skills and building a portfolio, and that publicly visible work can become training material for a system that competes with them, without their consent or compensation. The thing they need to do to attract clients—show their work—can also expose them to that competition.

So I wouldn’t measure the damage only by counting jobs that have already vanished. You also have to look at falling rates, less predictable income, and fewer opportunities for people starting out. Those pressures can make an artistic career unsustainable well before an entire occupation disappears.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lost commissions, falling rates, and unstable income, but does not say previously successful freelance artists fell into financial distress within roughly a year.

r002.rationale: It says clients may generate images cheaply, but does not specify that clients choose them despite flaws an artist can discern.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that, for freelance artists, this is about their livelihood. If you make your living doing commissions or illustrations, you don’t need AI to replace your entire profession to feel the damage. You just need some of your clients to decide that a generated image is good enough, or to use that option to push down what they’re willing to pay you.

And there’s a particular unfairness here: an artist’s work can become part of the training data for a system that then competes with that artist, without their permission or compensation. So they’re contributing something valuable, but they don’t get to negotiate the terms.

There’s also a longer-term concern. If the smaller jobs that sustain people early in their careers disappear, how do those people develop into established artists? The economic damage isn’t just a lost commission today. It can affect who gets to keep making art professionally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses livelihood and lost commissions, but does not say that previously successful freelance artists fell into financial distress within roughly a year.

r002.rationale: It mentions clients accepting generated images as good enough and using AI to push down pay, but does not identify low price as why clients choose images despite flaws that artists can discern.
